path: Sponsors run medical-emergency ads aimed at Republican women; Labrador and legislators keep up pressure over ballot language, but the measure stays on the ballot.
National money arrives on both sides. Right to Life and church networks frame it as 'abortion up to birth' and mobilize LDS and evangelical voters.
Republican midterm turnout dominates. Yes wins Boise and Blaine but loses rural Idaho clearly; the measure fails around 44-46%.
Trump endorses a loyalist; Norman self-funds and leans on his Upstate and York base, attacking the frontrunner as establishment.
The field consolidates into two or three serious contenders; Norman competes for the anti-endorsement vote with another conservative.
Low-turnout August primary: the endorsed candidate places first, and second is a close fight between Norman and another candidate.
Trump keeps a normal schedule of rallies, Truth Social posts and golf; no resignation talk.
Vance and the Cabinet stay loyal; Congress is in recess, and impeachment and the 25th Amendment are off the table.
No disabling health event or attack occurs; Trump remains president on August 31.
Owens keeps attacking Israel policy and TPUSA; Trump ignores her, not wanting to amplify her audience.
A reporter asks about Owens; Trump gives a dismissive but mostly non-insulting answer about her being entitled to views, or calls her 'a little off'.
Unless Owens targets his family directly, Trump stays mostly restrained; a borderline 'crazy' remark is possible but not certain.
Trade talks continue; asked about China, Trump calls Xi 'a very smart man' and 'a tough leader'.
A call or summit preparations with Xi keep China in the news, giving repeated chances for praise.
Even amid tariff friction, Trump praises Xi personally at least once during August.
Witkoff and Kushner hint that more countries are coming; Saudi Arabia still demands a Palestinian-state path.
A Central Asian or African candidate is courted, but the signing calendar slips toward the autumn and UNGA.
Without a firm White House ceremony, no new country formally signs by August 31.
Judiciary Committee schedules Blanche's process; Democrats attack his handling of the Epstein files, while Republicans stay united.
Swing senators raise questions but Thune holds the votes; Blanche keeps running DOJ as acting AG.
No fatal scandal emerges; Trump stands by his loyalist and there is no withdrawal by August 31.
Peace talks grind on; Putin offers no summit-worthy concessions, and Trump avoids a meeting without deliverables.
Zelenskyy pushes for a White House visit; Europeans propose joint talks, but August recess and Trump's travel reduce the chances.
Absent a ceasefire milestone, the two speak by phone but do not meet in person in August.
Leo XIV retreats to Castel Gandolfo; Trump and the Vatican have little direct contact.
Leo comments on migrants and on Ukraine and Gaza; the White House responds through Vance and Rubio, not a Trump call.
No publicized Trump-pope call or meeting is confirmed in August.
After the recall, Gibała launches as the anti-establishment favorite; KO picks a new, less-known candidate, and PiS fields its own candidate.
First round: Gibała leads, with the KO and PiS candidates splitting the rest; Gibała makes the runoff.
Runoff: right-wing voters back Gibała against KO, and he wins narrowly to moderately.
AfD leads at around 36-39%; Schwesig campaigns as the bulwark and draws tactical votes from CDU and Linke voters.
Greens and FDP hover below 5%, raising AfD's seat share, but SPD consolidates to the mid-20s.
AfD wins about 38% and roughly 42-45% of seats, short of an absolute majority.
AfD keeps a double-digit lead; the SPD duel framing narrows the gap somewhat.
A tactical SPD surge closes the gap to 5-10 points but does not overtake AfD.
AfD finishes first in seats; SPD is second.
Linke rides its national revival; CDU suffers from Merz's unpopularity, and BSW fades.
Some CDU and Linke voters defect to SPD tactically; both parties sit around 11-13%.
Third place is close; Linke edges CDU in about half of plausible outcomes.
AfD polls at 36-39%; small parties near the threshold create uncertainty over wasted votes.
AfD wins most constituencies; overhang and balancing seats enlarge the Landtag.
AfD lands near 28-33 seats; whether it falls inside 28-31 depends on the threshold misses and the chamber size.
SPD polls at 20-25%; Schwesig's personal popularity drives a tactical anti-AfD rally.
SPD rises toward the mid-20s but not to the 33%+ needed.
SPD gets about 19-24 seats, below the 26-29 bracket.
Linke surges on rents and young voters, competing with CDU for first place.
Greens and SPD lose voters to Linke; CDU holds the low-to-mid 20s.
Linke reaches about 20-24%, roughly 28-33 seats, short of 40 unless it reaches 28%+.
AfD polls at 14-17%, strong in the eastern districts.
CDU contains AfD in west Berlin; no major security shock occurs.
AfD gets about 15-17%, roughly 21-25 seats, well short of 35.
The Kremlin runs a managed multi-day vote with war-patriotism themes; KPRF campaigns softly.
Protest pockets in the Far East and Mari El exist, but administrative resources and tallies keep UR ahead.
The CEC reports UR first in every region, as in 2016 and 2021.
Yabloko struggles over registration; leaders face prosecution pressure.
If registered, it campaigns on peace but gets little media access; liberal voters are emigrated or suppressed.
Yabloko polls about 1-2% officially, far below 5%, or is kept off the ballot.
Abbott runs a well-funded campaign; the Democratic Senate nominee raises heavily in a Trump-midterm environment.
Polls show Abbott up comfortably and the Senate race closer, especially if Paxton is the Republican nominee.
Midterm backlash narrows the margins, but the Republican Senate nominee still wins Texas narrowly in most paths; the split occurs only in a strong wave.
The Supreme Court's ruling on Cook constrains at-will removal; Trump criticizes the Fed but pivots to the new chair.
A Trump-aligned chair reduces the urgency; no new formal removal of Cook is issued.
Unless the ruling invited a process-based retry, Trump does not formally re-fire Cook by September 30.
Brodie's decision shapes the race; if he retires, the field opens to slate-backed candidates including Howard.
Housing and the land-title controversy dominate; Howard competes with council veterans for the open seat.
With an uncertain field, Howard is one of several plausible winners; incumbent strength lowers his odds if Brodie runs.
Dyas runs on public safety and development; challengers emerge over housing and homelessness.
No single strong challenger consolidates the opposition in most scenarios.
Incumbency and low turnout carry Dyas to reelection, though a strong challenger could upset him.
Gillingham seeks reelection with business support; challengers attack him on taxes and crime.
The opposition remains fragmented among several candidates in first-past-the-post.
Gillingham wins reelection with a plurality.
Blekinge votes alongside the national swing; SD is strong, S is the largest party.
Coalition talks follow; the chair goes to the lead candidate of the winning bloc's largest party.
Hildingsson's chances depend on his party being that bloc leader; given unknown status, moderate odds.
Katsanidou leads the S list with the national red-green tailwind.
S plus partners likely retain a majority, or a cross-bloc deal keeps S in charge.
Katsanidou is re-elected chair when the new council convenes, unless the right bloc wins or she steps aside.
The Moderate-led bloc with SD support defends Skåne; Fritzon campaigns on healthcare.
The national swing to the left helps S, but SD strength in Skåne keeps the right bloc near a majority.
The right bloc most likely retains control; Fritzon wins only if the left-centre gains a majority.
Sörmland is competitive; the national red-green swing helps S.
Coalition formation decides the chair; Öqvist's party role is uncertain.
If Öqvist is the lead candidate of the winning side, he takes the chair; overall moderate odds.
S leads VGR; a succession question surrounds the chair's post.
The red-green bloc likely keeps a majority, but the nominee is uncertain.
Alnebratt becomes chair only if she is the selected lead candidate; that is uncertain.
Morell defends the right-centre majority; S campaigns on the national swing.
C and L weigh their options; the result is close between the blocs.
The right-centre narrowly loses ground; Morell retains the chair in somewhat under half of outcomes.
